conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. You’re here because you’ve been vomiting blood. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve had two episodes of vomiting blood in the last two days. It’s scary. I was just feeling better after my last hospital stay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. You mentioned at the ER that you were recently diagnosed with lupus and started on steroids. Can you tell me more about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, at the other hospital they said my blood work suggested lupus, gave me IV steroids for five days, and sent me home on prednisone. I was feeling great until two days ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And you’ve also had chronic abdominal pain and nausea for years. Did the prednisone help with that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It did, actually. For the first time in months, I wasn’t in pain. But now it’s back—same pain, nausea, and then the vomiting with blood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. We’ve checked your labs. Your hemoglobin is low at 10.7, but it’s stable. White blood cells are high, likely from the steroids. No sign of infection in your blood culture.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the blood in my vomit from an ulcer again? I had ulcers found on an EGD last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a possibility. We’ll schedule an EGD tomorrow to look inside. For now, we’re giving you IV fluids and continuing your prednisone. We’ve also restarted your Nexium to protect your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I also have this cold—sore throat, runny nose. I was on Augmentin, but it made me nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we saw you were on antibiotics. Since your symptoms are mild and it’s likely a viral URI, we’ll stop the Augmentin. We don’t want to irritate your stomach more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still nauseous, and I had another episode of vomiting, but no blood this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good—no fresh bleeding. Your labs are stable. We’re going to do the EGD today to check for ulcers or other causes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will they put me to sleep for it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll be sedated. It’s routine. They’ll also take a small biopsy from your duodenum, since you have a history of malabsorption.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you’re back from the EGD. The good news is no active bleeding. They saw a small hiatal hernia and some atrophy in the duodenum. Biopsies were taken.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No ulcers? But I had them before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No new ulcers. The previous ones may have healed. The bleeding might be from a small tear in the esophagus from vomiting—called a Mallory-Weiss tear. It often stops on its own.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I’ve heard of that. So it’s not serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not usually. Since your hemoglobin isn’t dropping, we’ll monitor you and keep you on stomach-protecting meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. You tolerated a soft diet yesterday without vomiting. How’s your pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. Still there, but not as bad. I’m glad I could eat something.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We did an abdominal X-ray yesterday. No blockage, but there’s a lot of stool in your colon. That could be contributing to your discomfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been constipated since the pain started. I’m not moving much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start a gentle laxative—senna—and docusate to help. Staying regular will help your gut feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your rheumatology workup came back. Most markers are normal. No clear evidence of active lupus here, but we’ll continue your prednisone as started.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But the other doctor said I have lupus. I’m confused.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know it’s confusing. Sometimes diagnoses are made based on symptoms and limited tests. Here, your ANA and other markers are normal. But since you were started on treatment, we don’t stop it abruptly. Your PCP will help decide next steps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll follow up with her.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. No more vomiting, pain is controlled. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What about my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue prednisone, but at a lower dose—20 mg daily. We’re switching from 60 mg. Don’t stop it suddenly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know, I’ve been on it before. What about the stomach medicine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll stay on esomeprazole twice daily. We’re also adding sucralfate four times a day to coat and protect your stomach lining.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And for nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving you Zofran tablets that dissolve under the tongue. Use them as needed for nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I like those.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re also adjusting your amitriptyline—from 50 mg to 25 mg at bedtime. It may help with pain and sleep but with fewer side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ve had dry mouth on it before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This dose might help. And keep taking your fludrocortisone and betaxolol for POTS.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t had dizziness, so that’s good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. Your condition is stable. No active bleeding, pain is manageable, and you’re eating well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I was worried about the bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. The EGD was reassuring. Keep taking your meds, especially the prednisone. Follow up with your PCP within a week to discuss continuing cellcept if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll call for my biopsy results from the EGD?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your GI doctor will contact you about those. If you vomit blood again, go to the ER. Otherwise, you’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and feel better soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—should I be worried about Sjogren’s? I was told I might have it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You mentioned a positive tear test and salivary issues as a child. But no biopsy was done. Your PCP may want to pursue that, especially with your family history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, my dad’s side has lupus and Sjogren’s. I’ll bring it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good idea. For now, focus on recovery. You’ve been through a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will go over your discharge instructions and prescriptions. You can leave once that’s done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it easy. Rest, stay hydrated, and follow up as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hope the prednisone keeps helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It should, but your doctor will monitor for side effects and decide if long-term treatment is needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Alright, I’ll let the nurse know you’re ready for discharge paperwork.
